title: Quantum Kernels and the Cross-Section of Stock Returns: Anatomy of a Vanishing Advantage
abstract: Do quantum kernels improve cross-sectional stock return prediction? We run a controlled horse race on the Chinese A-share market in which a quantum fidelity kernel, a projected quantum kernel, and a classical RBF control share identical training subsamples, solver, and tuning budgets, so that only the kernel is exchanged. On the main evaluation -- a point-in-time universe and 170 walk-forward windows (2012-2025) -- no quantum advantage exists: the fidelity kernel is indistinguishable from its RBF control ($Δ$IC $=+0.005$, $p=0.42$), and a $2\times2$ design crossing kernel type with training budget (a Nystrom extension to the full ~38,000-observation windows) shows quantum kernels matching, but never beating, equal-budget linear models; after family-wise correction no pairwise difference among eleven models is significant, with point estimates favoring penalized linear regressions throughout. We then document how the opposite conclusion arises: a 60-window evaluation on a universe screened with full-sample information makes the same quantum kernel appear dominant on stability criteria and significantly better than neural baselines. Interaction characteristics from the anomalies literature help nothing, quantum or classical; a widened bandwidth grid reveals an interior optimum rather than the near-classical endpoint a coarse grid suggests; and the geometric difference, while large throughout ($g \gg 1$), does not predict out-of-sample gains ($ρ=-0.20$). We propose protocol standards -- kernel-swap controls, budget-equalized comparisons, point-in-time universes, and multiplicity-robust inference -- for empirical claims of quantum advantage in finance.
summary: This paper rigorously tests if quantum kernels can predict stock returns better than classical methods using financial time series. The authors find that apparent quantum advantages are artifacts of flawed testing protocols, such as using hindsight data or unequal training budgets. They propose strict standards for future empirical claims of quantum advantage in complex systems.
main_problem: The study investigates whether quantum kernels provide a genuine, exploitable advantage over established classical machine learning methods for predicting cross-sectional stock returns.
main_result: Under rigorous, point-in-time evaluation protocols with sufficient statistical power, no statistically significant quantum advantage was found; penalized linear models consistently outperformed or matched the quantum kernel performance.
method: The authors employed a 'kernel-swap control' protocol, comparing Quantum Kernel Ridge Regression (QKRR) against classical controls like RBF kernels and linear regressions using walk-forward out-of-sample testing on financial data.
model_or_system: The system is the Chinese A-share stock market return cross-section. The models involve quantum encoding via an IQP-style layer to generate a fidelity kernel, which is then compared against classical kernels and linear predictors.
key_observables: Information Coefficient (IC), $\Delta$IC difference, $p$-values, Sharpe ratio, and the performance of various regression models over 170 walk-forward windows.
important_parameters: The evaluation is highly sensitive to protocols: point-in-time universes, budget equalization, and multiplicity correction are critical parameters for determining significance.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption tested is that the market structure allows for a stable, exploitable quantum advantage; the paper concludes this assumption is likely false due to methodological artifacts in prior literature.
figures_summary: Figures compare rolling IC differentials between quantum and classical kernels, showing how apparent advantages vanish when accounting for sample size or budget constraints.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem by testing QKRR against controls. It then details rigorous evaluation protocols (kernel-swap, point-in-time) across many windows, systematically debunking spurious quantum advantages through statistical corrections and diagnostic analyses of kernel geometry vs. out-of-sample gains.
why_interesting: While applied to finance, the methodology—developing strict protocol standards for claiming 'quantum advantage' in empirical data—is highly relevant to any field where theoretical quantum predictions meet noisy, real-world measurements (e.g., characterizing subtle effects in condensed matter experiments).
